analysis.one_liner: Lets dietary supplements carry disease and health claims without FDA approval or testing as drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing or vote: it was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee, and with zero cosponsors, never advanced before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal food and drug law to define vitamins, minerals, herbs, and similar products as 'dietary supplements' rather than drugs or food additives. It would have let makers put health and disease-related claims on labels and ads based on any evidence the company considered a reasonable basis, including unpublished evidence, and barred the Health and Human Services Secretary from requiring pre-approval of those claims. It also gave supplement manufacturers the right to sue in federal court to challenge FDA enforcement actions over their claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Dietary supplement manufacturers, distributors, and retailers gain the most. The bill removes the legal path under which a supplement marketed with disease claims could be treated as an unapproved drug, and removes substances in supplements from food-additive rules. It lets them advertise relationships between their products and diseases without pre-clearing the claims with the FDA, using a much lower evidence standard than drug approval, and gives them a court avenue to blunt enforcement. Consumers who want access to supplements and health information also gain latitude, but they would bear the risk that claims rest on thin or unpublished evidence.

how_it_helps.text: Defines a 'dietary supplement' broadly to include vitamins, minerals, herbs, and similar nutritional substances, and says a supplement cannot be considered a drug just because of the potency of its ingredients or because its labeling makes permitted health claims [S3].

Allows supplement labels and advertising to claim a relationship between the product and a disease or health condition if the claim is truthful and there is 'a reasonable basis' in scientific evidence, whether published or unpublished, and says uniformity of scientific opinion is not required [S3].

Bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from requiring that such claims be pre-approved by or conform to any FDA regulation before use, and gives manufacturers, distributors, and retailers a right to sue in federal court for a declaratory judgment when FDA challenges a claim [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on supplement labels and advertising bear the added risk: claims could rest on unpublished evidence and a 'reasonable basis' standard well below the proof required for approved drugs, with no FDA pre-approval to catch misleading claims. The FDA also loses a tool, since it could no longer require pre-approval and enforcement would trigger potential litigation by manufacturers.

drawbacks.text: The evidence bar for disease claims is low: unpublished evidence counts, uniformity of scientific opinion is explicitly not required, and no regulator reviews the claim before it reaches consumers [S3].

The bill forbids the Secretary from requiring pre-approval of health claims, so the first check on a misleading claim would come only after the FDA asserts noncompliance and the company chooses whether to contest it in court [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Consumers who want broader access to supplements and health information gain real latitude, and the low evidence bar is the point of the bill. The cost falls on the same consumers: with no pre-approval and a 'reasonable basis' standard that can rest on unpublished evidence, the burden of judging health claims shifts from the FDA to the shopper reading the label. The bill is designed around industry's dispute with FDA enforcement, and its consumer-protection tradeoff is substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 1992 with no cosponsors, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and sat there until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, never reaching a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1] [S4] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. William Dannemeyer (R-CA) introduced the Health Freedom Act of 1992 on July 7, 1992, late in the two-year Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and on July 24 to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill had zero cosponsors, and no committee, floor, or roll-call action ever followed; the Congress ended January 3, 1993, killing the bill [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, FDA retained its existing authority to treat supplements making disease claims as unapproved drugs and to require pre-approval of claims, and consumers kept the stronger labeling protections of current law; supplement manufacturers who wanted freer marketing gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: FDA authority and current consumer protections

for.name: Rep. William E. Dannemeyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to committee; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in a Democratic-controlled committee [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would let the industry market vitamins, minerals, and herbs with disease and health claims based on a 'reasonable basis' of any evidence, published or not, with no FDA pre-approval, and would shield supplements from drug and food-additive rules. Its gain comes at the cost of the pre-market review that catches misleading health claims before shoppers see them.
Supplements able to advertise against diseases without drug-approval requirements would compete with regulated medicines, while the bill leaves the drug approval pathway itself untouched.
